 Print US government is proposing one sentence change in USCIS rules that would change every H-1B visa extension form, with thousands losing their approval The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed a change to immigration rules that could make it harder for thousands of foreign workers to get their visa extensions approved. The change, one sentence long, would end a rule that requires US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to give weight to its own earlier approval when reviewing an extension request. The change could affect H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN, E and other work visa categories. According to immigration law firm Reddy Neumann Brown PC, the proposal is titled “Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility”. It was published on October 14, 2026. Public comments were due on November 13, 2026. What is the proposed USCIS change 
 Under the current rule, USCIS generally gives deference to an earlier approval when an employer files an extension for the same worker, job and underlying circumstances. This means the immigration officer usually relies on the previous decision unless there is a major error, a change in circumstances or new information that affects the worker’s eligibility. DHS now wants to remove this requirement by deleting Section 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) from the rules. If the proposal becomes final, USCIS officers could review an extension application from the beginning, even if the same employer and worker have already received approval for the same job. Officers would still be allowed to consider the previous approval, but they would no longer be required to give it special weight. It must be noted that the change does not mean that all existing visa approvals will be cancelled. Instead, it could make future extension applications more difficult and increase the chances of additional questions or requests for evidence. How many visa petitions could be affected
 DHS estimates that around 208,429 petitions filed each year could lose the benefit of deference to earlier approvals. H-1B petitions account for more than 75% of Form I-129 filings, according to the information cited by Reddy Neumann Brown PC. This means H-1B workers are likely to be among the most affected. The impact could be particularly significant for Indian professionals. According to USCIS data cited by the law firm, Indian-born workers accounted for 77.6% of H-1B approvals for continuing employment in fiscal year 2025. Will H-1B workers lose their visa extensions
 The proposed rule does not automatically mean that thousands of workers will lose their approvals. However, it could lead to more extension applications being questioned. USCIS officers could reopen issues that were already reviewed in an earlier application, such as whether a job qualifies as a specialty occupation or whether a worker meets the requirements for the position. DHS estimates that the change could result in around 6,044 additional requests for evidence (RFEs) every year. An RFE asks an employer or applicant to provide more information before USCIS makes a decision. The law firm also noted that DHS’s own analysis found no statistically significant difference in denial rates between periods when deference was applied and when it was not. The measurable impact was an increase in RFEs. How could the change affect workers
 More RFEs could lead to longer processing times for visa extensions. This could create uncertainty for workers whose employment depends on receiving an approval before their current status expires. Join conversation

 H-1B workers who file an extension on time can generally continue working for the same employer for up to 240 days after their I-94 period expires while the application is pending. Longer processing times could push more cases closer to this limit. The proposal could also affect international travel. Some workers wait for their extension approval before travelling abroad to obtain a new visa stamp. Delays could force them to postpone trips, including travel for family emergencies. Small businesses could face additional challenges as well. DHS data cited by the law firm shows that 57% of employers classified as small entities that filed H-1B extensions in fiscal year 2025 were small businesses. The median small employer filed just one petition.
